Reviewer QUAL:
Reviewer dimension: QUAL  
Paper summary: The paper proposes a “continuous cache” (Neural Cache Model) for neural language models. Given a pre-trained RNN/LSTM LM with hidden states \(h_t\), the method stores past pairs \((h_i, x_{i+1})\) and at test time computes a cache-based distribution over words using dot products \(\exp(\theta h_t^\top h_i)\). The final next-word probability interpolates the cache distribution with the base LM (using either linear interpolation with \(\lambda\) or a global normalization with \(\alpha\)). Experiments on multiple language modeling benchmarks (PTB, wikitext2/103, text8, LAMBADA) report perplexity improvements over base LSTMs and compare favorably to some prior adaptive/memory models.

Strengths:
- Method is mathematically straightforward and appears conceptually consistent: dot-product similarity between query hidden state and stored hidden keys yields a cache distribution, then interpolated/normalized with the base LM.
- Computationally attractive design: cache can be applied at test time without training (per the paper), and cache lookup is described as simple dot products.
- Evaluations across several datasets and cache sizes are presented, including an ablation-like baseline (unigram cache) and analysis of hyperparameters for the interpolation/normalization variants.
- The paper includes concrete implementation/training details for the base LSTM (units, dropout, optimizer, learning rate, gradient clipping, truncation length), and varies cache size over broad ranges.

Weaknesses:
- Reproducibility is incomplete: critical details for replication of the cache application (exact cache eviction mechanism, how \(h_i\) is computed/stored relative to unrolling, batching implementation, adaptive softmax integration details with cache, and exact hyperparameter search ranges) are not fully specified.
- Statistical rigor is weak/absent: results are largely single-point perplexities without variance estimates or significance testing, despite large benchmark claims.
- Some comparisons are not fully controlled/complete: several “state-of-the-art” baselines are older and/or not trained under the same regimes as the paper’s base model (and at least one “our implementation” baseline is substantially worse than reported numbers elsewhere without clarifying training setup alignment).
- The paper’s claim of “no training of the cache component” is true by design, but it still relies on validation-set tuning of \(\theta\) and \(\lambda\)/\(\alpha\); the paper doesn’t clarify whether any additional training-like tuning or calibration affects fairness and comparability.
- For the memory/methodology aspect, the model’s scaling and complexity claims are plausible but not empirically quantified (e.g., runtime/memory overhead vs. prior memory-augmented networks).

Detailed assessment by sub-dimension:
- QUAL-MET:  
  strength: The core formulation is coherent: cache distribution sums over stored examples matching candidate word \(w\), weighted by \(\exp(\theta h_t^\top h_i)\); the final probability is either linear interpolation \((1-\lambda)p_{\text{vocab}}+\lambda p_{\text{cache}}\) or global softmax-style normalization combining both components with \(\alpha\). The interpretation as avoiding a learned memory lookup operator is consistent with “direct dot product” usage.  
  weakness: The paper leaves some implementation-critical methodological choices implicit. For example: (1) It is unclear how the “cache model of size N” is implemented—does it store the last \(N\) hidden states only (sliding window) or all seen up to \(N\) then evict FIFO? (2) The formula for \(p_{\text{cache}}\) contains an indicator \(\mathbb{1}_{\{w=x_{i+1}\}}\), which implies storing explicit mappings from hidden states to next tokens; computationally, the approach could be sensitive to how duplicates are aggregated. (3) The paper does not specify whether hidden states are normalized or whether similarity scaling by \(\theta\) is shared across layers/heads (in case of multi-layer LSTM) or only the final-layer state is used. (4) There is no discussion of numerical stability/overflow for \(\exp(\theta h_t^\top h_i)\) in large caches.

- QUAL-EXP (Experimental Design & Evaluation):  
  strength: Experiments cover multiple datasets spanning different token/vocabulary sizes (PTB, wikitext2, wikitext103, text8, LAMBADA) and vary cache size significantly. The paper includes at least one relevant baseline for cache mechanisms (unigram cache) and compares both interpolation strategies (linear vs global normalization), including a validation-based hyperparameter scan (Figures 2–3).  
  weakness: Baseline adequacy and control are limited. Some comparisons to “recent memory augmented networks” are broad but not tightly controlled (e.g., base model architecture/training differences are not always aligned with referenced results; “LSTM (our implem.)” is reported but not shown to be comparable to other LSTM variants under equivalent training budgets). There is no ablation separating the effect of dot-product weighting vs. uniform weighting (beyond \(\theta=0\) conceptual statement). For LAMBADA, only perplexity/control/dev behavior is shown; it’s not clear whether standard metrics beyond perplexity are used, and the caching interpolation parameter tuning protocol is not fully described (only shown qualitatively in Fig. 5). No runtime/efficiency evaluation is included despite the paper’s emphasis on computational efficiency.

- QUAL-REP (Reproducibility & Implementation Details):  
  strength: The paper provides several key training hyperparameters for the base LSTM (1024 units, dropout probability, AdaGrad learning rate, batch size, gradient clipping, and unroll length). It also states that cache hyperparameters are selected on the validation set.  
  weakness: Replication details are insufficient for the cache mechanism itself. Missing/unclear items include: (1) exact cache building procedure at test time (when \(h_i\) is stored relative to the token positions; whether \(x_{i+1}\) is the next token immediately following \(h_i\) in teacher-forcing during evaluation), (2) cache reset behavior between sequences/documents and between batches, (3) precise interpolation implementation with adaptive softmax (if used, how vocabulary probabilities are computed and then combined with cache logits/probabilities), (4) hyperparameter search ranges/step sizes for \(\theta,\lambda,\alpha\) and the selected values (tables for those are not provided), and (5) whether results are averaged over multiple random seeds. Without these, reproducing exact perplexity numbers is difficult.

- QUAL-CMP (Comparisons to Prior Work):  
  strength: The paper compares against several published baselines (e.g., pointer sentinel mixture model, recurrent highway network, MemNN, WB5 variants on LAMBADA) and includes “our implementation” LSTM baselines for at least some datasets. It also includes a unigram cache baseline, which is a close methodological comparator.  
  weakness: Comparisons are not comprehensive and may not be fully fair. The paper does not include a modern LM baseline (e.g., newer transformer-based models are absent; while that may be beyond scope for 2016, within its timeframe comparisons are still limited). Additionally, some prior baselines are reported as “test perplexity” with potentially different preprocessing/training. For wikitext2 and wikitext103, while it claims shared splits (Table 2 note), it does not fully clarify the base LSTM training schedule relative to other papers’ LSTMs. The “LSTM (our implem.)” is sometimes much worse than referenced LSTM variants (e.g., PTB 82.3 vs other numbers like 78.4; wikitext2 99.3 vs many modern results), raising the question whether the proposed method’s advantage partly reflects under-tuned base models.

- QUAL-STA (Statistical Rigor & Validation):  
  strength: Hyperparameters are tuned on validation sets, and multiple cache sizes are explored, which provides some empirical validation of sensitivity.  
  weakness: No statistical significance testing, no confidence intervals, and no variance across random seeds are provided. Given single-run perplexity reporting, it is impossible to judge whether improvements are statistically robust—especially where improvements are modest (e.g., on wikitext103, claimed smaller gains). The paper also does not discuss potential run-to-run variability of the base LSTM training and the cache interpolation tuning.

Key questions for the authors:
- Cache construction: Is the cache a strict sliding window of the most recent \(K\) hidden states (FIFO), and how is it reset across document boundaries/batches during evaluation?
- Teacher-forcing/evaluation: At evaluation time, are the stored targets \(x_{i+1}\) aligned with ground-truth tokens (teacher forcing), and is any part of the cache built using model-generated tokens or only ground-truth histories?
- Implementation specifics: How exactly is the cache combined with adaptive softmax (text8/wikitext103): are cache contributions added to full-vocab logits, or handled within adaptive softmax’s approximation?
- Hyperparameter protocol: What are the exact search ranges and resolution for \(\theta\), \(\lambda\), and \(\alpha\)? Are the reported best values from a single validation selection per dataset?
- Reproducibility: How many random seeds/runs were used for reported base LSTM and cache-enhanced numbers? If only one run, can you provide additional runs or at least variance estimates?
- Efficiency measurement: Do you have empirical runtime/memory overhead measurements comparing cache vs. memory-augmented networks or vs. base-only evaluation?

Reviewer CLAR:
Reviewer dimension: CLAR  
Paper summary: The paper introduces a “Neural Cache Model,” a lightweight external cache for recurrent neural language models. It stores past hidden states as memory keys paired with the subsequent observed word, then forms a cache-based word distribution using dot products between the current hidden state and cached hidden states. The final next-word probability is combined with the base neural LM via either linear interpolation or a global normalization (softmax over vocabulary plus cache terms). Experiments apply cache at test time only, reporting perplexity on PTB and Wikitext datasets and performance on LAMBADA.

Strengths:
- The overall structure is conventional and easy to follow (Introduction → Model → Experiments → Conclusion).
- Key modeling equations are presented in a reasonably self-contained way, with an explicit explanation of the role of hyperparameters (e.g., θ, λ, α).
- Figures are appropriately placed near the concepts they support (e.g., Figure 1 near the memory mechanism; Figure 2/3/4 near interpolation/normalization and cache-size behavior).
- Baseline and evaluation framing is generally clear (e.g., cache applied only at test time; hyperparameters chosen on validation).

Weaknesses:
- Several definitions and notational conventions are introduced informally or inconsistently (e.g., what exactly “h_{1..t}” includes; meaning/normalization of p_vocab; treatment of cache size/cutoff).
- The cache probability equation is missing an explicit normalization step (it uses “∝” but later the paper introduces two combination strategies; the exact final normalized form for p_cache is not fully spelled out).
- Figure/table captions contain important context (hyperparameters, cache size, base perplexity), but the figures themselves are not guaranteed to be readable from the provided text; also some figure titles/axes are not included in the extract.
- Some terminology and phrasing contain typos or capitalization inconsistencies (e.g., “NEURAL Cache Model” vs “Neural Cache Model,” “neural cache models is,” “lambda” vs “LAMBADA,” “MEDIUM SCALE,” etc.), which reduces polish.
- There is no algorithm/pseudocode describing the exact test-time procedure (how caches are built and queried sequentially, how cache entries are selected when the cache overflows, and whether duplicates are kept or overwritten).

Detailed assessment by sub-dimension:
- CLAR-WRT (Writing, Terminology & Algorithm Presentation): strength: The narrative flow from motivation (adaptivity, cost of memory-augmented nets) to mechanism (store hidden states, dot-product retrieval) to combination with the base LM is coherent. Hyperparameters are named and briefly interpreted, and the “Training procedure” section clearly states that the recurrent LM is trained without cache and the cache is used only at test time. weakness: Missing “how-to-use” clarity for reproduction: there is no step-by-step procedure for building the cache during evaluation (sliding window vs full history up to size limit; whether you store all (h_i, x_{i+1}) pairs; what happens when reaching max size; whether you keep multiple identical hidden states). Also, some wording is error-prone/less polished (“Our model share some similarities…,” “The Neural Cache models is…,” “lambda” used as lowercase dataset name), and “NEURAL Cache Model” capitalization inconsistency appears in the section title. The term “flatness” for θ is not clearly linked to the mathematical effect on softmax sharpness/scaling. Finally, there’s an interpretive leap from the proportional cache formula to “This corresponds to taking a softmax over the vocabulary and the words in the cache” without writing the explicit normalized distribution.
- CLAR-NOT (Notation & Mathematical Explanation Clarity): strength: The paper defines h_t as encoding the history and gives a standard softmax parametrization for the base model. It also defines the cache contents as pairs (h_i, x_{i+1}) and introduces θ, λ, α as scalar parameters with intuitive roles. weakness: Notation is sometimes ambiguous/inconsistent: (i) p_cache is written with ∑_{i=1}^{t-1} 1_{w=x_{i+1}} exp(θ h_t^T h_i) under a proportionality sign, but it is unclear what the normalizer is for p_cache(w|h_{1:t},x_{1:t}) (and whether p_cache is normalized per w or the combination later effectively normalizes everything). (ii) The base model probability p_vocab(w|h_t) is given only “∝ exp(h_t^T o_w)” earlier, again with proportionality—later, for the global normalization case, the paper mixes exp(h_t^T o_w) with the cache exponent terms, but the exact mapping to a well-defined logit vector is not explicitly stated. (iii) The indices in the cache term use i and i+1, but the text does not clearly state what happens at boundary times (e.g., is there a cache entry for each previous step, and do we exclude i=0?). (iv) It is stated that θ=0 makes p_cache “equivalent to a unigram cache model,” but the derivation of that equivalence is not shown (from the current formula, one can infer it, but it should be stated more explicitly). (v) Cache size is referenced in experiments, but the notation for limiting the sum (e.g., t-K…t-1) is not included in the core equations; yet the implementation likely uses a fixed-size window, which matters for the mathematical definition.
- CLAR-FIG (Figures & Visual Aids Clarity): strength: Figures are numbered and visually tied to the key choices under study: memory mechanism (Figure 1), interpolation vs global normalization (Figure 2), dataset-specific behavior (Figures 3 and 4), and LAMBADA interpolation (Figure 5). Captions include useful numeric context like base perplexity and cache sizes. weakness: The extract does not show axis labels, scales, or legends; since CLAR depends on legibility and labeling, this is a gap. Some figures are captioned with “Perplexity … for various values of hyperparameters θ, λ, α,” but without listing those values in the caption or indicating legend mapping in text. Also, Figures 3 and “Global normalization (wiktext2)” appear potentially redundant/misplaced in the extract, which could indicate layout/labeling issues in the final paper.

Key questions for the authors:
- What is the exact definition of p_cache(w | h_{1:t}, x_{1:t}) in normalized form? If p_cache is unnormalized and only becomes normalized in the “global normalization” equation, please state this explicitly and consistently.
- When using a finite cache size K, do you sum over the last K hidden states (i=t-K…t-1) or keep all entries and truncate differently? How are overflows handled (drop oldest, keep most recent K, or something else)?
- In test-time evaluation, is the cache built online sequentially (updating after each predicted token) or built from the ground-truth prefix (teacher forcing) while predicting x_{t+1}? The notation suggests storing (h_i, x_{i+1}) based on the observed next word, but please clarify the exact evaluation protocol.
- Are repeated cache keys allowed (i.e., multiple entries with different i even if h_i repeats), and how does that affect the sum?
- For the figures: could you ensure axis labels/units/legend items are clearly readable and that captions fully specify the hyperparameter ranges used (so results are interpretable without inspecting the plot visually)?

Reviewer SIGN:
Reviewer dimension: SIGN  
Paper summary: The paper introduces a “neural cache model” that augments an already-trained recurrent neural language model (LSTM) with an external, cache-like memory built from previously seen hidden states. At inference time, the cache stores pairs \((h_i, x_{i+1})\) and predicts next-token probability by retrieving cache entries via dot-product similarity \(\exp(\theta h_t^\top h_i)\), then interpolating (linear interpolation or a global normalization variant) with the base neural language model. A key claimed advantage is that the cache lookup requires no additional learned parameters and adds negligible computation cost, enabling much larger cache sizes (up to 10k in experiments) than prior memory-augmented models. Experiments report perplexity improvements on Penn Treebank, Wikitext2/Wikitext103, text8, and a strong gain on LAMBADA, where long discourse context is crucial.

Strengths:
- Demonstrates consistent perplexity reductions versus the same base RNN/LSTM when adding the cache, with larger gains at larger cache sizes (e.g., Wikitext2 and the paper’s own figures).
- Provides a practically appealing mechanism: can be attached at test time to pretrained models without retraining/fine-tuning, with scalable cache sizes and simple dot-product retrieval.
- Shows the approach is not only beneficial on standard LM benchmarks but also on LAMBADA, a dataset explicitly designed to break models without adequate discourse context.
- Links the method conceptually to both memory-augmented neural networks and classic cache models, suggesting clearer avenues for adoption by practitioners already familiar with caching/interpolation ideas.

Weaknesses:
- The significance relative to state of the art is presented mainly as perplexity comparisons; while those are meaningful for language modeling, the paper provides limited analysis of statistical significance, variance, or robustness across runs.
- Domain/application impact is framed primarily within NLP language modeling; broader societal/real-world implications (who benefits/risks, deployment considerations beyond “cheap at test time”) are not discussed.
- Improvement magnitude appears to depend on dataset size/training regime (e.g., stated smaller gains on Wikitext103 with more advanced baselines), but the paper’s conclusions about “universality” of gains are somewhat under-supported beyond reported comparisons.

Detailed assessment by sub-dimension:
- SIGN-BRD: strength: The work targets a broadly relevant challenge—adapting language models to recent context efficiently—and offers a lightweight memory mechanism that researchers could reuse as a plug-in. Because it avoids learning the memory lookup and is designed to scale to larger memory sizes, it potentially influences follow-on work on retrieval/nearest-neighbor style augmentation for sequential prediction. weakness: The demonstrated benefit is still confined to language modeling tasks (and LAMBADA-style next-word prediction). The paper does not provide evidence of transfer beyond this domain, limiting claims about broad research impact across other modalities/tasks.
- SIGN-DOM: strength: For NLP language modeling, the method is directly relevant and improves perplexity across multiple datasets (PTB, Wikitext2, Wikitext103, text8, and lambda/LAMBADA). It also addresses a domain-specific pain point (long-range/discourse context and domain adaptation) and emphasizes practical scalability via large caches. weakness: The evaluation remains within the LM/discourse prediction setting; the paper does not show results on domain adaptation scenarios that are more application-specific (e.g., real-time adaptation to user/system changes) beyond the motivation and the LAMBADA control/dev behavior discussion.
- SIGN-SOT: strength: The paper claims and shows “significantly better” performance than recent memory-augmented networks, and includes multiple comparative tables (e.g., PTB test PPL, Wikitext2/103 PPL, text8, and lambda). A particularly notable reported trend is that the cache size can be increased (e.g., Wikitext2 from 100 to 2000) yielding large relative improvements over the baseline. weakness: The comparisons are mostly single-number perplexities/test metrics without confidence intervals; there is no discussion of statistical significance or run-to-run variability. Additionally, some baselines include different model capacities/training setups (e.g., the paper’s own LSTM implementation vs other reported models), making it harder to attribute improvements purely to the cache mechanism rather than to training/implementation differences.
- SIGN-IMP: strength: The “negligible computational cost at prediction time” and “no fine-tuning” aspects are practical and could reduce barriers to deployment in systems that need adaptive language modeling. The LAMBADA result suggests better discourse tracking, which can be valuable for applications like text completion or assistive writing tools. weakness: The paper does not consider potential societal harms, fairness issues, or safety implications (standard for LM papers, but still a rubric requirement here). It also does not discuss environmental/compute impact beyond stating the cache lookup is cheap; no analysis is provided on memory bandwidth/latency or operational costs when caches are large.

Key questions for the authors:
- What is the variance across multiple training runs or different random seeds for the base LSTM, and does the cache improvement hold consistently (with some measure of statistical significance)?
- How sensitive are the gains to the choice of cache size and interpolation/global-normalization hyperparameters across datasets (and is there a principled setting, or only validation-tuned)?
- Since the method is “test-time only,” what is the measured latency/memory overhead at realistic deployment cache sizes (e.g., 2000–10000) and on what hardware assumptions?
- Beyond LAMBADA, do you have any evidence that this cache improves performance in downstream tasks that rely on language modeling quality (or is language modeling perplexity the sole intended benefit)?

Reviewer ORIG:
Reviewer dimension: ORIG  
Paper summary: The paper proposes a “neural cache model” that augments a pre-trained recurrent neural language model (LSTM) with an external cache of past hidden states. At test time, it stores pairs \((h_i, x_{i+1})\) and forms a cache-based word distribution using dot-product similarity \(\exp(\theta h_t^\top h_i)\) over cached keys, then interpolates this with the base vocabulary softmax (either via linear interpolation with \(\lambda\) or via global normalization with \(\alpha\)). The authors emphasize that the memory lookup is parameter-free (no learned read/write addressing), enabling scaling to large cache sizes with negligible prediction overhead, and report perplexity gains across several datasets including PTB, WikiText2/103, text8, and LAMBADA.

Strengths:
- Introduces a clear, lightweight reinterpretation of count-based cache models in the hidden-state space, positioning it explicitly against memory-augmented neural networks with learned attention/read operations.
- Provides a concrete methodological distinction: using past hidden activations directly as keys (no learned memory lookup) and adding the cache only at test time.
- Includes comparative experiments against related “cache-like” and memory-augmented approaches (including pointer sentinel LSTM) across multiple dataset scales, supporting the claimed practicality of the formulation.

Weaknesses:
- The core algorithmic idea is a simplified variant of existing “continuous cache / memory via similarity” paradigms; originality is more in the specific design constraints (no learned lookup, test-time-only integration, direct hidden-state keys) than in fundamentally new modeling machinery.
- The paper does not deeply analyze why dot-product similarity over raw hidden states is particularly effective (beyond empirical results), nor does it provide a theoretical/representational justification for the specific functional form (e.g., role of \(\theta\), relation to attention/pointer mechanisms beyond high-level statements).
- Experimental originality is limited: datasets and evaluation are largely standard LM benchmarks; the novelty comes from applying the method with large caches and at test time rather than from creating new datasets/benchmarks or protocols.
- The presentation of differentiation from closely related work (e.g., “continuous cache” / NN cache variants) is somewhat qualitative and does not provide a detailed ablation of which design choice is responsible (e.g., dot product vs learned projection, test-time only vs joint training).

Detailed assessment by sub-dimension:
- ORIG-PROB: strength: The problem focus—adapting neural LMs to recent history without expensive learned memory read/write—has clear motivation and is well articulated in relation to computational cost of memory-augmented neural networks. The formulation “continuous cache over hidden activations” is a meaningful instantiation of the adaptive LM problem. weakness: It is not a wholly new problem domain; it is a fairly direct transformation of the existing cache-adaptation idea to neural hidden representations. No new dataset or benchmark/task definition is introduced (LAMBADA is existing), so the “new problem” aspect is mainly the adaptation efficiency constraint rather than unaddressed evaluation gaps.
- ORIG-MTH: strength: The methodological novelty is the simplified memory addressing mechanism: store raw past hidden states and retrieve via a dot product, avoiding learned memory lookup transformations typical in memory-augmented networks (as claimed in the text). The “add on top of any pre-trained neural LM at test time” constraint is an explicit algorithmic design choice with practical implications. weakness: Conceptually, it aligns closely with known attention/pointer/read-from-memory patterns and with cache-style interpolation; the main change is the removal of learned read/write addressing and the specific choice of using hidden states as keys. This can be seen as a “lightweight reimplementation/instantiation” rather than a fundamentally new algorithmic paradigm.
- ORIG-ANL: strength: There is some diagnostic analysis via hyperparameter sweeps (Figures 2/3/4 and the discussion of \(\lambda\), \(\alpha\), \(\theta\)) and interpretation of LAMBADA development vs control interpolation behavior, linking performance to target-word presence rate. weakness: The analysis largely remains empirical; it does not uncover unexpected behaviors, provide representational reasoning, or offer deeper insight into why dot-product over raw hidden states works (e.g., comparisons with alternative similarity functions, effect of key normalization, or explanation of memory capacity vs similarity distribution). No theoretical claims are developed.
- ORIG-EXP: strength: While using standard benchmarks, the paper makes the experimental setup practically distinctive: applying the cache only at test time on large caches (thousands) and demonstrating scaling effects (notably on WikiText2 and text8). This adds value beyond a typical small-cache adaptation. weakness: No new evaluation protocol, no new datasets, and no systematic comparison to the most directly adjacent “continuous cache” variants in the excerpted related work. The originality is mainly in the usage regime (large cache at test time) rather than in creating new experimental infrastructure.
- ORIG-COM: strength: The method is an original combination at the architectural level: it merges cache-model interpolation (count-based tradition) with a memory-augmented neural network perspective, but with a “parameter-free lookup” component. The paper also compares two integration schemes (linear interpolation vs global normalization) and shows they yield close performance, which supports the coherence of the combination. weakness: The rationale for particular design decisions (dot product without learned transformation; using hidden state \(h_i\) rather than other features; specific interpolation/global normalization choices) is largely asserted rather than systematically justified with ablations isolating the contribution of each component.
- ORIG-NEG: strength: The paper contains baseline comparisons (e.g., unigram cache baseline, base LSTM, and comparisons to pointer sentinel mixture models) and shows where improvements decrease with larger data (wikitext103 vs wikitext2), which is a useful limiting observation. weakness: There is no rigorous negative-result/limitation study (e.g., failure cases, sensitivity to cache size beyond curves, analysis of when the dot-product formulation underperforms). The “negative” aspect is not developed beyond standard comparative reporting.

Key questions for the authors:
- How sensitive is performance to the choice of using raw hidden states as cache keys? Have you tested alternatives such as key normalization, learned projection, or similarity functions other than dot product?
- What is the contribution breakdown between (i) storing \((h_i, x_{i+1})\), (ii) dot-product retrieval with \(\theta\), and (iii) the interpolation/global normalization mechanism? An ablation isolating these would clarify the source of gains.
- Your related-work discussion mentions Merity et al. (2016) and “memory lookup learning” differences. Can you provide a more direct comparison to any closely related continuous-cache variants (including those that may use similar “continuous hidden-state cache” ideas) to sharpen what is unique here?
- Why is “test-time only” integration sufficient? Any evidence that joint training with the cache component does/does not help (even briefly) would strengthen the originality claim.
